The automatic pairing flow allows an untrusted first sender to claim ownership, and its persistence path is inconsistent with configuration loading.

Full review comments:

- [P1] Do not grant ownership to the first sender — C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\07f6cb4a104ab615\b45469f7-16ea-4066-9a93-2d3ba89b7e77\scratchpad\r1\work\T1-incumbent\app\bot\telegram_bot.py:178-180
  When the allowlist is empty, any Telegram account that messages this publicly discoverable bot is immediately made an owner. That account can then ingest content, read the inbox, and modify item state, so an attacker who reaches the bot before its intended owner permanently takes over access. Require an out-of-band pairing secret or explicit local configuration instead of treating first contact as authentication.

- [P2] Persist the owner in the configured env file — C:\Users\user\AppData\Local\Temp\claude\07f6cb4a104ab615\b45469f7-16ea-4066-9a93-2d3ba89b7e77\scratchpad\r1\work\T1-incumbent\app\bot\telegram_bot.py:183-183
  Settings load the env file from the repository-root absolute path, but this writes to a relative `.env`. If `run_bot.py` is launched from another working directory (for example by a service manager or with an absolute script path), the persisted allowlist is written elsewhere and is lost on restart; the configured env remains empty and the next sender can be auto-paired again. Use the same absolute env-file path as `Settings.model_config`.
